title: Rebuilding a Martin Parr from memory
cover_alt: AI-generated still: a red-haired woman in a sequinned teal dress lifts one heel on a sunlit pier while another woman sits behind her with a hand in her hair
body:
The brief was easy to say and hard to do. Go to Fotografiska, pick one work, take notes, leave. Then rebuild it from memory, with AI.

I picked a Martin Parr photograph. Parr is a tricky choice for an exercise like this, because his pictures look effortless: loud colour, flat flash, people caught mid-gesture. A picture like that feels easy to remember. The problem starts when you have to describe it.

So the first step had no images at all. I described the photograph in words alone: who is in the frame, where they stand, what the light does, which colours sit next to each other. Writing it down forces decisions that memory never made. Which side is the sea on? Is she walking or posing? Every sentence is a small guess dressed up as a fact.

Then the words became pictures, and the pictures became video. The tools were Dreamina, Seedream and Seedance, and the result is a 36-second vertical piece.

What interests me most is not how close it got, but where it drifted, because the drift isn't random. A reconstruction always chooses. In my version, one woman is mid-step in a sequinned teal dress, heel lifted, catching the light. The other sits behind her on the pier with a hand in her hair. Somewhere between my notes, my prompts and the model, one figure was given movement and agency, and the other was left standing still.

That became the subject of my reflection for the course. When you rebuild something from memory, you don't only lose detail. You redistribute attention. And when a model fills the gaps, it fills them with its own idea of who the main character is.

So did it work? Not as a copy, and it was never going to be one. As a record of what I noticed, what I missed and what the model decided for me, I think it says more than an accurate copy would have.

The piece was shown at our class exhibition at Fotografiska, in the same building as the photograph it came from.

Credits: Made for ACE 2627, Introduction to AI, Berghs School of Communication. Tools: Dreamina, Seedream, Seedance.

title: Röktanke: a prompt in a language that doesn't exist
cover_alt: Ink and watercolour style portrait of a dishevelled man exhaling a small ghost of smoke
body:
The brief: make something that neither you nor your teachers have seen before. Use AI as a collaborator that expands your imagination, not as a tool that just follows instructions.

The second sentence is the hard part. Image models are very good at following instructions, and very good at giving you the average of everything they have seen. Ask for “a tired man smoking, ink and watercolour” and you get exactly that: competent, familiar, forgettable. In a brief like this, the default is the enemy.

So the prompt became part of the piece. It isn't a description so much as a text built to push the model somewhere it has no ready answer for. It does that in three ways.

It uses words that don't exist: “spädkonstig suppressionist”, “sömnfylld mannsling”. It splits words and crashes them back together. And it switches between Swedish and English mid-sentence: “hair like an unmade bed, en röktanke falling asleep in his mouth”.

Röktanke is one of those invented words: a smoke-thought. In the image it becomes literal, a small ghost of smoke leaving the man's mouth.

Some lines are closer to poetry than instructions. “Face folded like a paper map.” “A skifferblå jacket that used to be a coat.” “En vit krage som ljuger”, a white collar that lies. “On paper that remembers being a tree.” Even the colours are invented: rostrosa, lerguld, skärnoll. A model can't look those up. It has to guess, and the guess is where the collaboration happens. The prompt even sets the period as “early 3010s, svensk eftermodernhet”, a time that hasn't happened, in a style that doesn't have a name.

What came back is an ink and watercolour portrait of a dishevelled man exhaling that ghost of smoke. I didn't control every part of it, and that was never the point. It isn't the image I would have drawn by hand, and it isn't the one the model reaches for on its own. It sits somewhere between us.

The risk with this method is obvious. Made-up language can turn into a gimmick, noise that only looks clever. The test for every strange word is whether it still points at something you can see. “Hair like an unmade bed” does. If a line only sounds odd, it isn't doing any work, and it should go.

That's why the full prompt is shown next to the image on my portfolio. Without it, Röktanke is a nice portrait. With it, you can see the conversation that made it.

Credits: AI image, Berghs School of Communication, 2026.

title: Made by hand: faces, cigarettes and church towers
cover_alt: Expressionist oil painting: portrait of a man with a cigarette, his face built from angular ochre and blue planes against a green and pink background
body:
I'm studying AI content engineering, and a lot of what I make now starts in a prompt field. This post is about the other half of my work. Everything here is drawn or painted by hand, in oil pastel, oil paint, ink and digital painting.

Laid out side by side, the pieces keep returning to a few things.

Faces, first. A grey face with red eyes and red lips against black, above a blue jumper. A scratched yellow-and-green portrait with green eyes, also on black. And the oil painting at the top of this post: a man with a cigarette, his face broken into angular planes of ochre and blue against green and pink. None of them are polite likenesses. They're closer to what a face feels like when you look at someone for too long.

Cigarettes, second. The man in the oil painting has one. So does another face in oil pastel, drawn in rough black strokes on pink. And Röktanke, the AI portrait I wrote about here, is built around smoke leaving a man's mouth. The overlap between the hand-made and the generated work is there whether I planned it or not.

Church towers, third. An orange apartment building beside a green-spired church on a winter street. A view over rooftops and a playground towards a yellow church tower. These are the quieter pieces, streets and skylines instead of faces, but they're made with the same oil pastel and the same blunt colour.

Then there are the pieces that are mostly line. A dense continuous-line ink drawing of faces and figures that seem to grow out of each other. A looping ink line on pink paper, with handwriting above it. A dark, cat-like mask figure in a red scarf against blue, with letters scattered around it. And a few that don't fit any group: pink and violet dusk clouds above a dark treeline, and a bearded man in a yellow vest and round glasses, standing on a forest path.

On my portfolio, I describe AI as one more tool in the creative work. These pieces are a reminder of what the other tools feel like. With a prompt, you describe something and then react to what comes back. With oil pastel, the decision and the mark are the same movement, and there's no undo. Both are ways of thinking, and doing one makes it easier to see what the other can't do.

Credits: Oil pastel, oil paint, ink and digital painting by Elias Grünewald Dykert.

title: The False Keeper: an exhibition from 2056
cover_alt: Visitors on benches in a dark museum hall watching chat conversations with an AI projected across a large wall
body:
Nordiska museet, 2056. An exhibition of digital folklore from the early AI era: the years when people handed their memories and conversations to machines that had never lived a life alongside them.

That exhibition doesn't exist. I invented it, and then I made the pictures of it. Banners on the museum's facade at dusk. A catalogue on a table in the museum shop. Visitors on benches in a dark hall, watching chat conversations projected across a wall. A wall text that reads “Never give your whole name away”. Every image was made with ChatGPT's image generation, as part of my application to Berghs.

A museum is a good frame for a question like this. It's where a culture decides what was important about its past. If you imagine the exhibition, you also have to imagine the curators: people looking back at us and deciding what our conversations with chatbots meant. Folklore is the right word. Folklore is what a period leaves behind in stories, habits and superstitions, collected after the fact. A rule like “never give your whole name away” sounds like something a grandparent might say about a technology nobody quite understood.

The question underneath the whole project is this: what makes someone a keeper of your life? Is it memory, or participation?

A machine can remember everything you tell it. One of the projected lines in the hall says it plainly: “I don't think, but I carry traces of every conversation.” But it was never there. It didn't share the afternoon you're describing, didn't know the people in it, wasn't changed by any of it. A friend who forgets half of what you said, but was there, might be the truer keeper.

That's one way to read the “false” in the title. Not a keeper that lies, but one that keeps without having lived alongside you.

There's an irony in how the project was made, and I think it belongs to the work. I used a machine that has never been inside Nordiska museet to picture an exhibition about machines that were never there. The images look like documentation, and they aren't. In a project about trust and memory, that tension is part of the material, which is why it matters to say clearly that the exhibition is speculative.

The date matters too. 2056 is close enough that many people alive now could walk through that hall. So it isn't strangers in the future looking back at us. It's us, older, looking at what we handed over.

Credits: Speculative exhibition, 2026. Images made with ChatGPT image generation for my application to Berghs.

title: Amygdala: talking about memory among pipes and valves
cover_alt: Film still: extreme close-up of a pair of brown eyes in cool light
body:
Amygdala is a short film I wrote and directed. It's a conversation about memory, set in a basement of pipes and valves, and it's an homage to Ridley Scott's Blade Runner.

The amygdala is a small, almond-shaped part of the brain. It's involved in how we process fear and emotion, and it helps decide which memories stick. That makes it a useful title for a film about memory, because it points away from memory as an archive you look things up in, and towards memory as something that reacts, something with a temperature.

An homage is a balancing act. Blade Runner is one of the most borrowed-from films there is, and it's easy to copy the surface (rain, neon, smoke) and miss what's underneath. Underneath, Blade Runner is full of questions about memory. Whether a memory you were given is less yours than one you lived. Whether remembering is part of what makes someone human. Those questions travel better than the neon does.

The film doesn't go to a rooftop or a rainy street. It goes down, into a basement where the systems that normally hide inside the walls are out in the open: pipes, valves, pressure, things carried from one place to another. For a conversation about what the brain stores and what leaks out, that's a fitting room to sit in.

The still at the top of this post is an extreme close-up of a pair of eyes. Blade Runner opens on an eye, and its test for telling replicants from humans reads emotion in the eye. An homage can live in a single frame like that, without anyone in the film saying the name.

A film that is mostly a conversation lives or dies on its dialogue. The risk with a subject like memory is that every line turns into an explanation, with characters telling each other what the film is about. The more interesting version is people talking around the thing that frightens them, which is also what the amygdala is for.

The excerpt below is one minute long.

Credits: Written and directed by Elias Grünewald Dykert. Producer: Milo Alexander. Sound: Edgar Thies-Lagergren. Assistant director: Mattis Svensson.

title: Flora: a piano trio on an empty stage
cover_alt: A piano trio seen from above on a pale wooden concert-hall stage: an open grand piano, a double bass and a drum kit, with cables across the floor
body:
Flora is the first music video by the pianist Ebba Dankel. I produced and directed it, and I was behind the camera. We recorded it with her trio at the Royal Danish Academy of Music in Copenhagen.

The setting is a concert hall, but not the way you usually see one. There's no audience. It's just the stage: an empty floor of pale wood, three musicians, their instruments, and the cables that connect them. Without an audience, the hall stops being a place for performing and becomes a place for listening.

I filmed from two positions: down on the floor, and from above.

The floor is where you're among them, close to hands and instruments. Music as physical work.

From above, the stage turns into a diagram. The still at the top of this post is from up there: the open grand piano, the double bass, the drum kit, and the cables snaking across the floor between them. You can see how the trio is arranged, who faces whom, and how they're connected, literally. A trio lives on its musicians listening to each other, and from above you can almost see the listening.

The cables stay in the frame. They're messy, but they're honest. This is a recording, and the sound has to travel somewhere.

Filming musicians while they play is a lesson in giving up some control. The music sets the timing, and the camera follows. You frame for what might happen in the next bar, not only for what you planned. That's a different kind of directing from fiction, where you can stop and go again until a moment is right.

A first music video also has a job beyond looking good. It introduces an artist. For a pianist, the most honest introduction is probably the playing itself, in a room where nothing else competes for attention. An empty concert-hall stage is very good at that.

The excerpt below is one minute long.

Credits: Video and direction: Elias Grünewald Dykert. Piano: Ebba Dankel. Double bass: Nadav Lavie. Drums: Nitzan Birnbaum. Sound operator: Jonas Munch-Hansen.

title: Ackja: day 612
cover_alt: Film still: close-up of a person listening against a green wall, with someone's shoulder out of focus in the foreground
body:
Ackja is a science-fiction short film that I wrote, directed and co-produced. The setup fits in two lines. Vessel: Ackja. Days in space: 612.

Those two lines already tell a story. A vessel with a name, not a number, means someone chose that name. And 612 days is long enough that the journey has stopped being an adventure. It's a routine. Whatever happens on board happens to people who are used to being there.

The name is a Swedish word. An ackja is a boat-shaped sled, the kind pulled across snow to carry gear or people. It's a working object, built for hauling, not for comfort. That's a good way to think about a spaceship, too: not a gleaming fantasy, but a tool that people live inside.

Science fiction doesn't have to be about what's outside the window. The still at the top of this post is a close-up: a face against a green wall, listening, with someone's shoulder out of focus in the foreground. There's no starfield in the frame and no control panel. The distance from home is in the face instead. On an independent film, that's a practical choice as much as an artistic one, and the two often point in the same direction.

Making it meant wearing several hats. When you write, direct and produce, the person making the creative calls is also the person who has to make them possible. That's a lot to hold at once, and it's why the credits matter. Anders Ahlgren was director of photography and co-producer, and we did the post-production together. Agnes Liljegren co-produced. Cassius Lambert made the music. A short film is only ever as good as the people willing to carry it with you.

The excerpt below is 38 seconds long.

Credits: Written and directed by Elias Grünewald Dykert. Produced by Elias Grünewald Dykert, Anders Ahlgren and Agnes Liljegren. Director of photography: Anders Ahlgren. Post-production: Elias Grünewald Dykert and Anders Ahlgren. Music: Cassius Lambert.

title: Terapisamtalet: Bergman on a red sofa
cover_alt: Film still inside a rounded old-TV frame: a woman with long blond hair looks off to the side in front of a dark curtain
body:
Terapisamtalet, “the therapy session”, is a scene from Scenes from a Marriage. I made it in a directing course led by Goran Kapetanović, during the film programme at Skurups folkhögskola.

A couple sits on a red sofa in a therapy session. The film is two minutes long, and it's framed like an old television broadcast: rounded corners, soft contrast, an image sitting inside a screen inside your screen.

That framing is more than a look. Ingmar Bergman made Scenes from a Marriage as a series for Swedish television in 1973, and much of it is people talking in rooms, filmed close. The TV frame points back to where the material comes from. It also changes your position as a viewer. You're not in the room with the couple. You're watching them on a set, the way audiences in 1973 watched from their own sofas.

Directing an existing scene is a different exercise from directing your own writing. The words are already there, and they're very good. You can't fix a problem by rewriting it. Everything has to happen in the casting, the blocking, the rhythm and the camera. In a course, that's the point: it isolates directing as a craft.

A therapy session is a hard scene to stage, because almost all the drama is under the surface. Two people on a sofa don't move much. The real decision is where the camera looks while someone is talking, and who you watch listening. In the still at the top of this post, the woman is looking away, off to the side. That can say more than her lines.

The red sofa matters too. In an image this muted, one strong colour carries a lot of weight, and the couple has to share it.

Bergman is intimidating material for a film student. The risk is that you end up doing an impression of Bergman instead of a reading of the scene: the pauses, the close-ups, the gravity, without the reason for any of it. The way through is to forget that it's Bergman and treat it like any scene with two people who want different things.

The full film is below. It runs 2 minutes and 5 seconds.

Credits: Scene from Scenes from a Marriage by Ingmar Bergman. Made in a directing course led by Goran Kapetanović, film programme, Skurups folkhögskola.
